description: team of one, at least for now
summary:
CosmicFeed is a social media inspired feed for NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey. It turns real infrared images of the sky into posts anyone can scroll, compare and question, with no telescope, account or FITS files needed.

Our server pipeline searches NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive (DR1 and QR3), downloads small cutouts, and lines up every date onto one north-up grid. It removes zodiacal light and saves each post as a draft for human review before it goes public. Visitors can blink between survey dates in the Discovery Lab, watch time-lapse reels, and flag anything that seems to move. Each flag is checked against known-object catalogues. An optional colour view follows NASA’s own SPHEREx colour mapping (830 nm, 1.7 µm, 4.8 µm), choosing exposures by the exact wavelength SPHEREx recorded at each spot. A watchlist job adds new survey dates automatically.

The challenge asks how SPHEREx data could help find unknown moving objects, including a possible Planet X. Spotting them means comparing the same sky across dates, a task that needs many eyes. CosmicFeed makes that comparison quick and familiar, and it is honest about what is unconfirmed. That opens NASA’s newest sky map to the public and turns casual scrolling into real citizen science.
details:
What it does

CosmicFeed turns NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey into a social feed. Each post is one patch of sky with two or more SPHEREx survey dates behind it. Visitors scroll the feed, watch time-lapse Reels, and open the Discovery Lab to blink between dates, compare them side by side, or drag a reveal slider, with zoom and pan synced. If something seems to move, they press and hold to flag it. Flags are checked against known-object catalogues (IMCCE SkyBoT for asteroids) and go into a review queue with four honest statuses: Awaiting Review, Community Flagged, Under Scientific Review and Identified. A Sky Map built on Aladin Lite shows NASA’s SPHEREx DR1 all-sky map with every post pinned in place.

Why this approach

People already spend their attention on feeds. Adults worldwide spend about 141 minutes a day on social media (DataReportal, 2025). In the US, 84% of adults use YouTube, 71% use Facebook and about half use Instagram (Pew Research Center, 2025). TikTok users watch roughly 92 short videos a day, in sessions of about 11 minutes (Sensor Tower). Scrolling, double-tapping and swiping are among the most practised skills on Earth.

Citizen science has shown that this kind of attention can do real science. Galaxy Zoo collected more than 50 million classifications from over 150,000 volunteers in its first year, and they matched professional astronomers’ accuracy. Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 is the closest example to ours. More than 100,000 volunteers flipped through infrared WISE images looking for objects that move, found over 1,500 nearby stars and brown dwarfs, and earned co-authorship on scientific papers. CosmicFeed uses that same proven method on NASA’s newest survey, SPHEREx. It moves it from a desktop task page to a phone-first feed people already know how to use.

How it works

SPHEREx images are 70 MB+ FITS files behind an archive that is often slow, so visitors never touch it. Our server pipeline works ahead of time:

  • It looks up each target with CDS Sesame and applies its proper motion.
  • It searches NASA/IPAC IRSA (DR1 and QR3) for every frame covering that spot and picks one frame per six-month survey.
  • It downloads small cutouts and decodes the FITS files with our own TypeScript reader.
  • It subtracts the zodiacal-light model and resamples each image through its TAN-SIP WCS onto one shared north-up grid. Blinking then shows real motion, not pointing drift.
  • Finally it stretches and saves a small PNG.

A Python engine (Astropy, reproject, NumPy) handles bulk ingestion and cleans cosmic-ray hits. GitHub Actions schedules refresh a watchlist of fast-moving stars and brown dwarfs. Every post arrives as a draft, and a person reviews it before it goes public.

The optional colour view follows NASA’s own SPHEREx colour mapping: 830 nm as blue, 1.7 µm as green, 4.8 µm as red. SPHEREx’s filter changes wavelength across its detector, so we use each detector’s wavelength table to pick exposures where the target was actually seen at those wavelengths. The legend shows the measured values.

Benefits and intended impact

The challenge notes that comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and possibly new planets reveal themselves by shifting between images, but no one person can check a billion objects. CosmicFeed spreads that work across many people. Even a small community adds up. As an illustration only: 1,000 people spending 5 minutes a day at about 10 seconds per field would make roughly 30,000 checks a day, more than a small science team could look at in a year. It needs no software, telescope or astronomy training, and it works on a phone.

We want it to:

  • Bring NASA’s newest sky map to students and the curious public.
  • Give researchers a stream of pre-sorted candidates.
  • Teach how astronomers really find moving objects: by comparing the same sky over time.
  • Turn some of the time people already spend scrolling into a contribution to science.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript and Python.
  • Web app: TanStack Start, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query.
  • Data: Supabase (Postgres, storage, row-level security) through Lovable Cloud.
  • Astronomy: Aladin Lite, Astropy, reproject, NumPy.
  • Data sources: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA, cutouts, HiPS), CDS Sesame, IMCCE SkyBoT, JPL Horizons.
  • Testing and automation: Vitest and Testing Library for tests, GitHub Actions for scheduled jobs.
  • Development: Lovable and Claude Code.
  • Hardware: none. Everything runs in the browser and on serverless functions.

What’s creative about it

I treated a research dataset like social media. Every SPHEREx field becomes a post, “did anything move?” becomes a one-tap question, and time-lapses become Reels. Under that familiar surface is a real science pipeline, including a FITS and WCS reader written from scratch to run in a serverless function. I also built a colour view that follows NASA’s wavelength choices exactly instead of inventing colours.

What we considered

  • Honesty: no fake discoveries. Flags are “candidates”, AI answers can’t call a change confirmed, AI illustrations are labelled, and every real image carries NASA/JPL-Caltech/IPAC credit and a link to its source file.
  • Scientific accuracy: aligned grids, proper-motion correction, cosmic-ray cleaning, and colour by real wavelength.
  • Reliability: images are prepared ahead of time, so NASA’s archive outages never break the app.
  • Accessibility: works on phones, tablets and desktops, and flagging works with a thumb.
  • Privacy: flag positions are public, but who flagged them is not.
  • Limits: SPHEREx is shallow, so a very distant Planet X is unlikely to be bright enough to see. Backyard Worlds hasn’t found Planet 9 either. The tool is best suited to nearby fast-moving stars, brown dwarfs and Solar System bodies, and we say so rather than overpromise.

Sources: DataReportal/We Are Social (2025) via Statista; Pew Research Center Social Media Fact Sheet (Nov 2025); Sensor Tower TikTok usage data; Zooniverse Galaxy Zoo results; NOIRLab and NASA on Backyard Worlds: Planet 9.
